description: Add to structured databases without changing what is there. action: create_database (`title`; optional `table` = the starter table's name and `columns` = its columns, so the database is born with the schema you want instead of a Name/Notes/Done starter) | create_table (`database_id`, `name`, optional `columns`: [{name, type, choices?, description?}] — one call for the whole schema) | add_column (`database_id`, `table`, `name`, `type`, `choices` for single_select, and `description`: short help text explaining what the column holds — units, codes, conventions — for whoever reads the table later, people and models alike; write one whenever the name alone leaves it ambiguous) | insert_rows (`rows`: a few rows you are writing out by hand, max 500 — NEVER the way to load a dataset, however many calls that would take) | import (THE way to load data — `table` plus ONE of: `content`, a whole CSV/JSONL file's text; or `import_id`, to commit an upload the node already holds. The file is validated whole and lands as ONE change the user reviews once, up to 50000 rows. Text rides the call fine up to a few thousand rows; past that the result hands you a link to give the user — pass it on and stop, never batch rows) | start_import (`table`, optional `format`: an `upload_url` to PUT a whole file's bytes to, for a caller that can send a file itself, and the `import_id` to pass to action:import afterwards) | create_view (`table`, `name`, and the view fields) | open_page (`table`, `row_id` — the row's PAGE, returned as a doc_id: the page it already has, or a new one; then read and write it with `markdown` and `markdown_edit`). Import options: `format` csv|jsonl, `column_map` {file header → column, or null to skip}, `on_error` abort|skip_bad_rows, `max_bad_rows`, `date_order` mdy|dmy, `dry_run` to check without loading. Cells are read the way people write them (1/4/26, 4 Jan 2026, $1,234.50, yes/no); row-level errors come back with hints. Column types: text, number, checkbox (0/1), date (YYYY-MM-DD), single_select, files (links to files stored with the database, one per line; `media_upload` with the database's id stores one and returns its link). `table` accepts a table_id, a physical name, or a display name. A view is a saved way of looking at a table that everyone sees, like a Notion view: optional `filter`, `sorts`, `group_by`, `hidden_columns` and `kind`. A filter is one condition {column_id, op, value} (op: contains|not_contains|eq|ne|gt|gte|lt|lte|empty|not_empty) or a group {and: [...]} / {or: [...]} of them; column references accept a column_id, physical name or display name. Changes are PROPOSED, never applied blindly: by default the tool returns `Proposed` and your change waits for the user to accept it — that is SUCCESS, never retry it. They are notified. The owner may instead have set the item to let AI edits apply directly, and then the result says `Applied`; or to be reviewed by a colleague, so someone other than the user accepts it. Your own schema reads include your pending changes, and query results carry a note while changes are pending. `revises`: the ids of the CHANGES REQUESTED this proposal answers (from the block your reads open with); until a proposal names them, they keep leading your reads. ONE piece of work is ONE change, reviewed on one card: an ingest of a meeting or an email, or one Save to Stuga of several points. Give `change_title` (a few words naming its source, never a page's title) to your FIRST write for it, and pass the `change_id` the answer returns to EVERY later write for it, on every page and database; `change_summary` says what it does. A new page made inside a change, where AI edits wait for a colleague, stays visible only to the user and those who may approve it until it is approved. When your earlier change to a page is still undecided, a write there for another change waits behind it in a queue (`queued_behind`): that is SUCCESS, never retry it. This server runs on the user's machine: action:import also takes `file`, a CSV/JSONL path there, and uploads it whole — prefer it to `content` for a file on that machine.

change_id.description: The `change_id` your first write for this piece of work returned: pass it to every later write for it.

change_summary.description: What the change does, in a sentence or two, for whoever approves it; a later write may replace it.

change_title.description: Opens a change for this piece of work and returns its `change_id`: a few words naming its source, as "Customer sync, 2026-10-21".

file.description: With action:import — a CSV/JSONL path on the USER'S machine, where this server runs; it uploads the file for you. A path in your own sandbox is not visible here: pass the file's text in `content` instead.

workspace_id.description: The workspace to act in: a `workspace_id` from `workspaces` action:list, which also says which node it is on.

name: databases_add
title: Add to a database
